prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Mathematical Notation Reference (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Symbol" · longest unbreakable word 54px · one-line width 54px
  col 2: header "Name" · longest unbreakable word 78px · one-line width 105px
  col 3: header "LaTeX" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 4: header "Meaning" · longest unbreakable word 100px · one-line width 1191px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 360px (different strategies, not small variations).
An earlier design attempt for this table was rejected by independent reviewers. Their comments: another layout was rated acceptable: All columns fit in the viewport and the symbols, names and LaTeX are easy to scan. The narrow Meaning column creates very tall rows and splits words such as ‘antiderivatives’ and ‘construction’. | another layout was rated good: The identifying columns stay readable and the wider Meaning column keeps words intact with less wrapping. Reading the descriptions requires horizontal scrolling. | your previous preferred design was rated acceptable: The wider Meaning column gives the prose a more comfortable measure, but more of each description lies beyond the viewport, increasing the cost of comparing it with the symbol and name. | another layout was rated bad: Equal-looking narrow columns waste space on short symbols while splitting names and many words in the descriptions. The resulting tall rows are difficult to read. | another layout was rated good: The identifiers remain intact and the descriptions wrap without the conspicuous word splits seen in A. A small amount of horizontal scrolling is needed to see the ends of some lines. | another layout was rated good: The identifiers stay intact and the Meaning column keeps words together. Only a small part of the table extends beyond the viewport, although some line endings still require scrolling.
another layout was rated bad: Equal-width columns leave Meaning extremely narrow, splitting many words and making the rows very tall; even Summation breaks. | another layout was rated acceptable: The table fits the viewport and keeps the names and LaTeX commands readable, but Meaning is still narrow enough to split words such as antiderivatives and construction. | another layout was rated good: The wider Meaning column preserves words and gives the descriptions a more natural rhythm, while names and commands remain intact. Reading the ends of lines requires horizontal scrolling. | another layout was rated good: Names and commands stay intact, and the descriptions wrap without the conspicuous word splits seen in B. A small amount of Meaning extends beyond the viewport. | another layout was rated good: The first three columns remain clear, and Meaning has enough width to preserve words with only a small horizontal overflow.
